passages.t: Build houses, seek the city's peace, and plans for a future
passages.happening:
This is the letter Jeremiah sent from Jerusalem to the elders, priests, prophets and all the people Nebuchadnezzar had taken to Babylon (verse 1), after King Jeconiah, the queen mother, the officials and the craftsmen had gone (verse 2). It went with Elasah and Gemariah, whom Zedekiah sent to Nebuchadnezzar (verse 3).

“Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat their produce” (verse 5). They are to marry and have sons and daughters and increase there, not decrease (verse 6). ‘Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf, for if it prospers, you too will prosper’ (verse 7). They must not be deceived by the prophets and diviners among them, for God did not send them (verses 8 and 9).

When Babylon's seventy years are complete, God will come to them and bring them home (verse 10). ‘For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope’ (verse 11). Then they will call on him and pray, and he will listen (verse 12). ‘You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart’ (verse 13). He will be found by them and bring them back from captivity (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The letter was sent some time after the deportation of 597 BC. The exiles were not scattered as slaves. Many were settled in communities of their own in the Babylonian countryside, such as Tel-abib by the Chebar canal, where Ezekiel lived. Business records from a village called Al-Yahudu, Judahtown, show Judean exiles living as tenant farmers there.

Building a house, planting a garden and marrying a wife were the three basic acts of settling down in Israel's world. The law exempted a man from war if he had just done any of them. Jeremiah uses that language on purpose: put down roots. The prophets among the exiles were telling them to keep their bags packed.

To pray for the welfare of Babylon, the city that had burned their homes, was a startling command. The word for welfare is shalom. The exiles' own peace was bound up with the peace of the city where they lived.
passages.later: Moses had promised the same: ‘you will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul’ (Deuteronomy 4:29). Paul tells believers to pray ‘for kings and all those in authority’ (1 Timothy 2:2).
passages.hard:
Can a reader claim Jeremiah 29:11 as a personal promise that God will prosper them and not harm them?

Start with its first readers. The promise was given to the Judean community in exile, and the you is plural throughout. It came with a hard condition of time: it would be fulfilled only after seventy years (verse 10), which meant most adults who first heard the letter would die in Babylon. The plans to prosper and not to harm were God's plans for the people's future as a whole, brought home under Cyrus decades later, not a promise that each reader's circumstances would soon improve. The letter was written to answer prophets who promised quick relief.

That does not make the verse empty for readers today. It shows God's character: he has purposes of peace for his people, he keeps his promises across generations, and he is found by those who seek him with all their heart. The misreading is to treat it as a guarantee of personal success or of a problem solved soon.
passages.asks: The exiles were told to plant gardens in a land they did not choose. Ask where God might be asking you to put down roots instead of waiting to leave. And ask whose peace you could pray for, even if they once hurt you.

passages.t: False prophets in Babylon, and Shemaiah's letter
passages.happening:
The exiles say that the LORD has raised up prophets for them in Babylon (verse 15). But God says that the king on David's throne and the people still in Jerusalem will face sword, famine and plague, like figs too rotten to eat (verses 16 and 17), because they did not listen (verse 19).

God names two prophets in Babylon, Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, who prophesy lies in his name. He will hand them over to Nebuchadnezzar, who will put them to death before the exiles' eyes (verse 21). Their fate will become a curse among the exiles (verse 22), for they committed outrage in Israel, adultery with their neighbors' wives and lies in God's name (verse 23).

Shemaiah the Nehelamite, in Babylon, sent his own letters to Jerusalem, telling the priest Zephaniah that he ought to lock up Jeremiah for writing that the exile would be long (verses 24 to 28). Zephaniah read the letter to Jeremiah (verse 29). God says that Shemaiah has prophesied without being sent and made the people trust in a lie, so neither he nor his descendants will see the good God will do (verses 31 and 32).
passages.hearers:
The exiles had prophets of their own who promised a quick return. Jeremiah's letter had to compete with them, and with messages sent back to Jerusalem.

The two prophets named in verses 21 to 23 were condemned for their lies and their lives. Their death at Nebuchadnezzar's hand became a proverbial curse. The chapter names it in a line and moves on, and these notes do the same.

Shemaiah tried to use the temple's chief officer to silence Jeremiah. The priest Zephaniah instead read the letter to Jeremiah himself. A letter meant to end Jeremiah's ministry brought another word from God.
passages.later: Ezekiel, among the same exiles, sat with them ‘seven days’ (Ezekiel 3:15) before he spoke. Daniel later prayed from Babylon, having read Jeremiah's seventy years (Daniel 9:2).
passages.asks: Shemaiah tried to silence Jeremiah because his message was unwelcome. Ask whether you have tried to silence a hard word instead of weighing it. And ask whether the voices you trust are the ones that tell you what you want to hear.
